rv.q: Though Santiago-Hudson doesn't pull off a production that keeps that engine consistently blazing, he — as a superb actor of Wilson himself — does make space for us to meet these people in all their fullness. And that's not nothing.
Like a great blues composition, Seven Guitars finds beauty in sorrow, humor in hardship and poetry in pain.
Director Ruben Santiago-Hudson’s connection to August Wilson is evident in this deeply intimate, leisurely, and strong 30th-anniversary revival of Seven Guitars.
Santiago-Hudson has assembled an ensemble full of Wilsonian actors that could hardly be bettered
Wilson’s lyrical feel for Black-American life is enough of a special effect in and of itself.
In their characters’ varied reactions to the rooster crowing in a neighbor’s backyard, a cast of seven exemplary performers illuminates Black life in the Hill District of Pittsburgh in 1948

This revival is simply stunning. Santiago-Hudson presents us a haunting production that’s not just absorbing, charged, and emotional but one that brings music to a level I have never seen before in a play. The musicality of the performance pours from the stage through dialogue, instruments, and the movement of the cast across the stage.
As in any blues number, Seven Guitars succeeds on the strength of an ensemble that blends well even as it astonishes us with its sudden variations.
August Wilson’s Seven Guitars begins at a graveside yet makes room for bawdy laughs, unrequited love, and a bluesman who refuses to live his life without.

cn.t: Critics celebrate this Lincoln Center revival of August Wilson's *Seven Guitars* as a triumph, praising Santiago-Hudson's direction and the magnificent ensemble cast bringing Wilson's poetic, blues-infused portrait of Black Pittsburgh life to breathtaking life.
